strengths: Conceptual unification: Formulating local test prediction variance (TPV) as the trace form Tr(H_eff C) establishes a clear and intuitive bridge connecting disparate phenomena—sharpness/SGD noise, quantization robustness, benign overfitting under label noise, and network pruning—under a single analytical lens.

Rigorous distinction: The paper provides conceptual clarity by contrasting local prediction variance around a fixed solution w* with classical global prediction variance over retraining, demonstrating why local perturbations around a trained model exhibit different dynamics.

Theoretical contribution on TPV stability: Theorem 3.1 provides an interesting guarantee that training-set TPV approximates test-set TPV in the overparameterized limit without requiring test labels, and Theorem 4.2 provides a neat spectral characterization of label noise sensitivity in nonlinear networks.

Extensive empirical verification: The authors conduct thorough experiments across 300+ synthetic configurations, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, and text classification with BERT, systematically mapping out where TPV stability holds and where it breaks.

Actionable practical utility: The paper successfully leverages TPV stability for training-set-only hyperparameter/recipe selection across multiple regularizers and for deriving JBR, a label-free structured pruning criterion that matches or exceeds established baselines.
weaknesses: Theoretical gap between assumptions and real-world behavior: Theorem 3.1 relies on an isotropic covariance assumption (C = sigma^2 I) and infinite-width NTK stability, whereas actual perturbations (e.g., label noise, pruning masks) induce highly anisotropic covariances. Furthermore, empirical stability holds even at width = 1, suggesting that the NTK stability mechanism does not fully explain why TPV stability persists in practice.

Computational overhead of empirical estimation: Evaluating empirical label-noise TPV requires multiple (R = 5 to 20) independent fine-tuning runs on perturbed logits because direct inversion/conjugate gradient of the Jacobian is ill-conditioned in deep networks (Appendix D.3.3). This renders TPV estimation considerably heavier than single-pass sharpness or gradient-based diagnostics.

Regime dependence for model selection: As shown in Figures 7 and 9, the correlation between TPV and test error follows a U-shaped curve, meaning TPV only tracks generalization in the low-training-loss / overfitted regime and inverts under underfitting. This requires practitioners to verify training loss convergence before relying on TPV rankings.

Incremental algorithmic novelty in pruning: The derived JBR pruning metric is mathematically equivalent to the existing Jacobian Criterion (JC; Chen et al., 2025) on correctly classified samples, limiting the standalone algorithmic novelty of the pruning application.

strengths: Unifying Conceptual Framework: The paper provides an elegant perspective by formalizing Test Prediction Variance (TPV) as the trace functional Tr(Heff C), cleanly decoupling the data/model Jacobian geometry (Heff) from the specific perturbation mechanism (C).

Insightful Jacobian-Spectral Characterization: Theorem 4.2 and Section 4.1 provide a clear explanation for why standard loss sharpness (dominated by large singular values of the Jacobian) and label-noise sensitivity (dominated by small singular values) can decouple or even exhibit inverse correlations, resolving apparent paradoxes in how regularization affects different noise types.

Extensive Empirical Investigation: The authors evaluate empirical TPV stability across an impressive breadth of settings, including 324 synthetic configurations, multi-width MobileNets and ResNets on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet architectures, and BERT models on text classification tasks.

Decoupling of TPV Stability and Generalization: The empirical demonstration that training-set TPV tightly mirrors test-set TPV across multiple orders of magnitude, regardless of the generalization gap and even down to width=1, is a fascinating and practically relevant finding.

Exemplary Scientific Honesty: Appendix D.3 candidly details the numerical failure of conjugate gradient methods due to extreme Jacobian ill-conditioning (condition numbers of 10^6–10^8), transparently acknowledging why the idealized linearized object cannot be solved directly in deep networks.
weaknesses: Gap Between Theoretical Formulation and Empirical Evaluation of Label Noise: While Theorem 4.2 analyzes the minimum-norm stationary point of the linearized system around w*, the practical algorithm used in the experiments (Appendix D.3.4) performs multi-epoch non-linear fine-tuning with SGD/AdamW without proximity regularization (gamma = 0). This departs from the first-order Taylor regime and minimum-norm assumption that form the mathematical backbone of the paper.

Isotropic Assumption in Theorem 3.1 Contradicts the Main Motivations: Theorem 3.1 (and Theorem A.5) establishes TPV trace stability strictly under the assumption that the perturbation covariance is isotropic (C = sigma^2 I_p). However, the primary perturbation sources of interest—label noise (C = sigma^2 V S^{-2} V^T), SGD noise (Lyapunov solution), and structured pruning (group rank-1 blocks)—are inherently highly anisotropic. As a result, Theorem 3.1 does not provide formal theoretical coverage for the main experimental settings.

Asymptotic Limit Inconsistency in the Proof of Theorem A.5: In Step 2 (page 14), Lemma A.4 applies the standard Law of Large Numbers for a fixed finite-dimensional space R^{p x p} as n_X -> infinity, obtaining an operator-norm gap bounded by p * o(1). However, the overparameterized NTK setting requires the width m -> infinity, which implies parameter dimension p -> infinity. Treating p as fixed while invoking the LLN and subsequently taking m -> infinity requires uniform random matrix concentration bounds that are not formally established.

Incremental Novelty of the JBR Pruning Criterion: As discussed in Section H.1, the proposed JBR criterion is essentially identical to the Jacobian Criterion (JC) of Chen et al. (2025), with the sole difference being the substitution of ground-truth labels with the model's predicted class (pseudo-labeling). Framing this via TPV is conceptually consistent, but the practical pruning contribution is largely an incremental modification of existing OBC/JC pipelines.

Practical Limitations of TPV-Based Model Selection: Because the relationship between TPV and test loss is U-shaped, TPV only correlates positively with test loss in the low-training-loss regime and inverts when models underfit. In practice, determining whether a model is safely past the argmax-TPV threshold requires either tuning over training loss thresholds or computing training trajectories, and the correlation weakens noticeably in cross-architecture comparisons (as seen in Figures 10 and 25).

strengths: Unifying Conceptual Framework: The paper provides an elegant, cohesive lens connecting multiple distinct post-training phenomena—including wide minima under SGD noise, benign overfitting under label noise, quantization error, and structured pruning—via the trace formulation Tr(Heff C).

Thorough Empirical Investigation: The empirical study is comprehensive, spanning synthetic benchmarks (324 configurations), CIFAR-10/100 across widths and depths, ImageNet backbones, and NLP fine-tuning with BERT.

Transparency and Discussion of Failure Modes: The manuscript openly analyzes and documents regimes where TPV stability breaks down (e.g., large noise variance in Figure 5, numerical ill-conditioning in Section D.3.3, and the sample size dependency in Figure 2).
weaknesses: Theoretical Gap in Theorem 3.1: The stability guarantee (Theorem 3.1 / A.5) relies on the assumption of isotropic covariance C = sigma^2 I. However, the realistic perturbation sources studied in the paper—such as label noise (rank r <= n << p), SGD stationary noise, and group pruning masks—are severely anisotropic, degenerate, and data-dependent. Thus, the formal theory does not directly cover the primary perturbation settings analyzed in Section 4 and evaluated in the experiments.

Breakdown under Noise Interpolation: For label noise, if an overparameterized model interpolates or closely fits the noisy targets, TPV_train trivially collapses to sigma_epsilon^2, whereas TPV_test depends on the Jacobian spectrum and continues to vary across architectures (as illustrated in Figure 5). Label interpolation is a hallmark of modern overparameterized networks, so characterizing this as a 'pathological case' downplays a common regime.

Practicality and Overhead of Model Selection: Computing empirical label-noise TPV requires running R (5 to 20) independent fine-tuning runs of multiple epochs on the training set (Appendix D.3.4). In practice, if a practitioner has sufficient compute to retrain the network multiple times, holding out a standard validation split is typically far more computationally efficient and direct. Furthermore, because the TPV–test loss relationship is U-shaped (underfitting vs. overfitting branches), TPV cannot serve as an unambiguous model selection criterion without external knowledge of the training loss regime.

Incremental Novelty in Applications: The theoretical derivations under SGD noise and quantization essentially recover well-known classical results (e.g., Mandt et al., 2017; Zhu et al., 2018). Furthermore, the proposed JBR pruning metric is an incremental modification of the Jacobian Criterion (JC) from Chen et al. (2025), differing primarily by replacing ground-truth labels with the model's predicted class labels.

strengths: Unifying perspective: The paper aims to provide a common conceptual lens—Test Prediction Variance (TPV), framed as the curvature-covariance interaction Tr(Heff C)—to analyze a variety of perturbation mechanisms such as SGD stationary noise, label noise, quantization, and pruning.

Extensive empirical exploration: The authors conduct extensive experiments across synthetic benchmarks, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet architectures (ResNets, MobileNetV2, VGG) exploring the empirical relationship between training-set and test-set prediction variance.

Competitive practical heuristic: The proposed Jacobian-Based Rebalancing (JBR) structured pruning method is label-free and demonstrates competitive performance against established baselines in the OBC framework.
weaknesses: Flawed proof of the central theoretical result (Theorem 2.1 / Theorem A.4): In Appendix A.1 (Equation 22), the paper claims that because Heff(w; X) = (1/n) J^T J and G_X(w) = (1/n) J J^T share their non-zero eigenvalues, the operator norm bound ||G_X(w*) - G_X(w0)||_op <= eps implies ||Heff(w*; X) - Heff(w0; X)||_op <= eps. This deduction is mathematically invalid: for two matrices A and B, ||A A^T - B B^T||_op <= eps does not imply ||A^T A - B^T B||_op <= eps because the eigenspaces can rotate independently. Furthermore, Lemma A.3 applies the standard finite-dimensional Strong Law of Large Numbers to p x p matrices while taking the overparameterized limit p -> infty without dimension-free concentration bounds.

Conceptual misinterpretation of 'TPV stability at width = 1': The authors treat the observation that TPVtrain ≈ TPVtest holds tightly for width = 1 as unexpected or paradoxical relative to their overparameterization theorem. However, for a given perturbation delta w, TPV is simply the empirical average of a squared prediction difference (f_{w*+delta w}(x) - f_{w*}(x))^2. For width = 1, the network has minimal capacity, so uniform convergence of empirical sample means to population means over n = 1000 samples follows from basic statistical learning theory. Presenting this as evidence of an overparameterization phenomenon reflects a misunderstanding of basic sample concentration.

Limited novelty in noise derivations and pruning algorithm: The derivation linking SGD covariance to Hessian curvature via the continuous Lyapunov equation (Theorem 3.3) is largely identical to existing derivations in the literature (e.g., Mandt et al., 2016/2017; Thomas et al., 2020). Additionally, JBR (Section 3.4) differs from the Jacobian Criterion of Chen et al. (2025) merely by substituting ground-truth labels with the model's predicted class (standard pseudo-labeling).

Disconnect between theoretical formulations and empirical implementation: As detailed in Appendix C.3.3–C.3.4, the idealized closed-form label-noise expression cannot be evaluated via iterative linear solvers (such as CG) due to severe ill-conditioning (spectral condition numbers of 10^6–10^8). The empirical validation must rely on heuristic local SGD fine-tuning with proximity penalties, ad-hoc mini-batch freezing, and eval-mode constraints, significantly diluting the connection between the derived theory and empirical results.

strengths: The paper aims to offer an ambitious, unifying perspective that connects multiple distinct post-training phenomena (SGD stationary fluctuations, label noise sensitivity, quantization error, and structured pruning) through a local prediction variance functional of the form Tr(Heff C).
The authors conduct a broad set of empirical evaluations across synthetic setups, CIFAR-10/100, and ImageNet, sweeping widths, depths, sample sizes, and perturbation types.
The paper is generally well-structured and clearly written, providing detailed descriptions of experimental protocols and implementation considerations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Fatal mathematical flaw in the core theoretical result (Theorem 2.1 / Theorem A.4): In Appendix A.1 (Eq. 22), the authors assert that because the empirical NTK Gram matrix GX(w) and the parameter-space feature covariance Heff(w; X) share their non-zero eigenvalues, the operator-norm bound ||GX(w*) - GX(w0)||op <= epsilon implies ||Heff(w*; X) - Heff(w0; X)||op <= epsilon. This statement is mathematically false: the operator norm of the difference between two Gram matrices A A^T - B B^T does not bound the operator norm of A^T A - B^T B, because the alignment of their eigenvectors in R^p can differ substantially. Furthermore, Lemma A.3 applies the standard finite-dimensional Strong Law of Large Numbers in Frobenius/operator norm for Heff in R^{p x p}, which is invalid in the overparameterized asymptotic limit where width m -> infty implies parameter dimension p -> infty (far exceeding sample size n).

Conceptual conflation regarding 'TPV Stability': The authors express surprise that empirical TPV stability holds tightly even for width = 1 and only breaks when sample size n is small. In Eq. (17), for a fixed trained network and perturbation distribution R, empirical TPV is simply a sample average of the function g(x) = E_R[(f_{w*+delta w}(x) - f_{w*}(x))^2] over i.i.d. draws from the underlying distribution D. By the standard Law of Large Numbers / Central Limit Theorem for Monte Carlo integration, the sample mean over 1,000 training points and 5,000 test points drawn from the same distribution D must concentrate around the same population expectation regardless of network architecture or width. Framing standard Monte Carlo sample-mean concentration as a deep-learning-specific trace stability phenomenon decoupled from generalization is conceptually misleading.

Limited novelty in noise analysis: Several of the derived relations are essentially known in the literature. The SGD stationary noise result (Theorem 3.3) reproduces established trace-based noise-curvature relationships from stochastic optimization literature (e.g., Mandt et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2020), while the quantization result (Remark 3.4) is a direct application of standard second-order Taylor expansion under isotropic independent noise.

Marginal originality and heuristic nature of JBR pruning: The proposed JBR pruning criterion (Section 3.4) is virtually identical to the Jacobian Criterion (JC) of Chen et al. (2025), differing solely by replacing the true label y(x) with the one-hot predicted class label e_{c(x)}. Using pseudo-labels for label-free or data-free pruning is a well-known heuristic, and the empirical improvements over JC are minor.

Intractability and ad-hoc workarounds for label-noise TPV: As acknowledged in Appendix C.3.3, deep-network Jacobians are severely ill-conditioned (condition numbers 10^6 - 10^8), causing conjugate gradient solvers to fail completely. The resulting perturb-and-retrain proxy requires extensive manual interventions (disabling batch norm/dropout, fixing random mini-batch sequences, discarding runs with high Taylor error or non-decreasing loss), which weakens the claim that TPV provides an accessible, robust theoretical metric.

strengths: The paper presents an ambitious attempt to unify diverse parameter perturbation phenomena—such as SGD stationary noise, label noise, finite-precision quantization, and structured pruning—under a single mathematical formulation based on the curvature-covariance trace $\mathrm{Tr}(H_{\mathrm{eff}} C)$.
The empirical evaluation is extensive in scope, featuring broad sweeps over synthetic setups, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet across different network widths, sample sizes, and architectures.

The manuscript is clearly structured and transparently documents empirical limitations, including the severe ill-conditioning of Jacobians in modern deep networks and the conditions under which empirical TPV stability breaks down (e.g., in Appendix C.3 and Section 5.2).
weaknesses: Conceptual and technical novelty is limited. The first-order Taylor expansion of prediction change $\mathbb{E}[\|f_{w^*+\delta w}(x) - f_{w^*}(x)\|^2] \approx \mathrm{Tr}(H_{\mathrm{eff}} C)$ is a well-established tool across multiple subfields, including Bayesian deep learning / Laplace approximations, SGD noise and diffusion analyses (e.g., Mandt et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2020), second-order quantization error modeling, and classical pruning (OBD/OBS). Similarly, Theorem 3.2 is simply the standard minimum-norm least-squares variance formula applied to linearized features (the Jacobian), which mirrors classical results in overparameterized linear regression and NTK regression.

Theoretical gaps in the proof of Theorem 2.1 (TPV Trace Stability). The proof of Lemma A.3 relies on the finite-dimensional strong law of large numbers in Frobenius norm in $\mathbb{R}^{p \times p}$ to argue that $\|H_{\mathrm{eff}}(w_0; X_{tr}) - H_{\mathrm{eff}}(w_0; X_{te})\|_{op} \to 0$. However, the NTK regime requires width $m \to \infty$, which implies parameter dimension $p \to \infty$. In the overparameterized regime where $p \gg n$, operator-norm convergence of sample second-moment matrices cannot be justified by standard finite-dimensional LLN without explicit dimension-free operator concentration bounds. Furthermore, the upper bound scales with $\mathrm{Tr}(C)$; for isotropic noise where $C = \sigma^2 I_p$, $\mathrm{Tr}(C) = p \sigma^2 \to \infty$ as $m \to \infty$, rendering the bound vacuous unless scales and limits are handled rigorously.

Questionable interpretation of empirical TPV stability across widths. The authors express surprise that TPV stability holds tightly even at width = 1. However, for extremely narrow models (e.g., width = 1), function capacity is minimal, so uniform convergence trivially ensures that empirical training statistics concentrate around their population expectations. Conversely, as acknowledged in Section C.2 and Figure 7, when an overparameterized model actually overfits training perturbations (e.g., higher $\sigma$), training TPV deviates significantly from test TPV and stability breaks. Hence, empirical TPV stability appears largely driven by either the smallness of the perturbation (avoiding overfitting) or standard sample averaging, rather than an overparameterization-specific phenomenon.

Marginal contribution in the pruning application. The proposed JBR pruning criterion is almost identical to the Jacobian Criterion (JC) of Chen et al. (2025), differing only by replacing true targets with model argmax predictions on confident samples ($p > 0.9$). In the empirical evaluations (Figures 9, 10, 15, and 16), the performance trajectories of JBR and JC are virtually indistinguishable across all sparsity levels, offering minimal practical or empirical advancement.

High computational cost for empirical estimation. As described in Appendix C.3, exact computation of the label-noise TPV requires inverting ill-conditioned Jacobians, which fails in practice, necessitating multiple perturb-and-retrain fine-tuning runs. If multiple retraining runs are required to compute empirical TPV, it provides limited practical utility as a label-free diagnostic of generalization relative to standard evaluation methods.
